items.title: Duet
items.meta: Cal Hacks 11.0 · First place grand prize
items.note:
At my first hackathon, my team and I built Duet, a brain-computer interface that turns brainwaves into music in real time. You put on an EEG headset, and signals related to your focus and calm help shape the music being composed. We ended up winning the First Place Grand Prize at Cal Hacks 11.0!

But getting there was a whole story.

I’d only been learning to code for about a month when I applied. I honestly didn’t know what a hackathon was going to be like, but my mentor told me that at her first one, she made the slides and did all the pitching. That made me think, ok, maybe there’s something I can bring to this too coming from a pure business background at that point.

When I got accepted, I was super surprised and happy. Then I remembered I didn’t have a team.

I opened the Slack and everyone seemed so cracked. Meanwhile, I was trying to figure out how to pitch myself with a month of coding experience. I noticed someone from Ottawa, looked at her profile, and saw we had a lot of mutuals. So I reached out to friends to see if I could get an introduction.

My pitch was basically that I was really good at case competitions and could help us present and sell whatever we built. That was the strongest thing I could offer at the time, so I went with it. She actually said yes! We started reaching out to more people and eventually teamed up with two Stanford students.

One teammate had the idea to use brain-computer interfaces. I didn’t even know what a BCI was yet, but I was down to figure it out. The first problem was that we didn’t have a headset. We started reaching out to BCI companies in SF to ask if we could borrow one, and Emotiv said yes!

I still had to convince my parents to let me go, though. I had midterms the day after the hackathon (which I conveniently didn’t mention), and I didn’t have enough money for the trip. I asked my brother if he could spot me, and he told me I’d better not be going all the way there just to network. So I told him I was going to win - Completely pulled that out of my ass. But now I had a headset, a team, and a promise to keep.

[Photo: picking up the headset or testing it for the first time]

Once we picked up the headset, I started learning how it worked. EEG measures electrical activity through sensors on your scalp, and we could use the headset’s software to access the data. I’d never worked with hardware like this before, so even getting signals onto a screen was pretty exciting.

We eventually landed on music. One teammate knew about BCIs, and Justin and I both had music backgrounds and had taught students for years. It was something we understood enough to start experimenting with. 

It also got us thinking about the applications: students who couldn’t easily express themselves through words or instruments. What if they could participate in making music through signals from the headset?

By the time I got to the opening career fair though, my confidence from that conversation with my brother had disappeared. I was so scared to talk to anyone. Full imposter syndrome. I basically sat alone at a table waiting for my teammates, who were finishing their midterms and arrived late that night.

That night, I slept on the ground with my clothes as makeshift bedding. I was freezing and remember thinking I was definitely going to get sick.

[Photo: my sleeping setup for night one]

Once we started building, the biggest challenge was getting the music to respond live. We wanted someone’s state to influence what was being composed as they listened. However, this was a novel idea (to us at the time) and we couldn't find anyone who's previously done this type of generation before.

The headset streamed data into our Python backend through Emotiv’s Cortex API, with SingleStore supporting low-latency processing. We used signals related to focus and calm to guide musical qualities like tempo, rhythm, and intensity.

Gemini was our live composer. It received the current state and context about what it had just played, then decided what should come next. Sonic Pi performed the music.

This was one of the coolest parts of the project for me. With procedural generation, we could have written rules mapping particular inputs to musical patterns. Here, the model was making musical decisions as the session unfolded. We still had to connect those decisions to something that could actually play, and get the whole loop responding quickly enough to feel interactive.

I built the Next.js frontend to show the brainwaves alongside the music. It was also my first time using Claude, which helped me turn our Figma designs into a working interface. A month earlier, I’d been learning the basics of coding. Now I was trying to get a frontend working with an EEG headset and an AI music pipeline.

[Image: the interface, followed by a diagram of how the system worked]

Meanwhile, we kept having to find somewhere to work.

The Wi-Fi was bad on the second day, so we went to a teammate’s former office. We worked there and stayed overnight, but in the morning security thought we were intruders and nearly called the police on us.

We moved again, this time to a hotel near the Metreon. Then we almost missed demos and were running back and forth trying to make sure we could secure a booth. By this point, getting ourselves and the project to the right place was its own challenge.

[Photo: our office or hotel workspace]

During demos, one teammate went around telling people to come try Duet while the rest of us ran the booth. After spending the weekend learning the headset and connecting all these pieces, we finally got to see other people put it on and hear the music.

Then we won first place.

Somehow, I’d actually kept that ridiculous promise to my brother.

[Photo: the team after winning]

Afterwards, my team and I had some really cool opportunities arrive at our doorstep. We got to speak with music schools to demo and also received an invitation to demo at IIT Bombay Techfest, which is the largest asian tech festival (ex. the Dalai Lama would go to this). 

To anyone who's thinking of doing a hackthon, you should do it! If you can sleep on the ground wihtout anything for one night, you could probably do anything.

P.S. I almost failed my exams but it was worth it

items.title: SolarScope
items.tags: Swift, Python, AR, computer vision, Arduino
items.note:
SolarScope was my second hackathon project, an AR app that lets you visualize solar panels on an existing building and estimate their potential efficiency. We built it at Hack Western and somehow ended up winning Best Hardware Hack!

Coming back from Cal Hacks, I wanted to take what I’d learned and try it again closer to home. I was a lot less scared this time, but apparently still very interested in making things difficult for myself by choosing another hardware project.

The idea started with my friend Xander, who’d worked on a research paper about solar panels with his professor (shoutout to Xander, I’ll link his paper here!). I had a background in sustainability, so I wanted to explore whether we could turn some of that research into something people could actually use.

What if you could put on AR glasses, look at a building, and see what a solar installation might look like?

[Link: Xander’s research paper]

At Cal Hacks, reaching out to companies had helped us borrow an EEG headset. So I tried the same thing again, this time with AR glasses companies.

Got rejected by all of them.

I don’t think I explained what we were trying to do very well. In my head, the idea made sense, but getting someone else to understand it well enough to lend us hardware was a different challenge. Definitely a lesson in making my pitch clearer.

I also went into this one without a team, but I was much more confident about finding people. Instead of stressing over everyone’s profiles on Slack, I found my teammates at a Hack Western mixer the day before.

We decided to go for the idea. Since we couldn’t borrow glasses, we ordered a pair from Costco with the intention of returning them afterwards.

Apparently we never did, so that was fun.

[Photo: the team or our hardware setup]

The project had a few pieces we needed to connect. Computer vision would help analyze the building and guide solar panel placement, AR would show what the installation could look like, and solar calculations would give an estimate of its efficiency.

We were also using an Arduino to detect sunlight. I think it was everyone’s first time working with one, so we were learning the hardware while trying to get it working with the rest of the project.

The interesting challenge was connecting something physical, the sunlight measurements, with a visualization that someone could use to explore an installation. Seeing panels on a building was one part of it. Giving people information about how that installation might perform was another.

But getting everything working through the glasses proved harder than we expected.

Eventually, we had to change the plan for the demo. We moved the AR visualization onto a phone and kept the glasses setup for detecting sunlight. The experience was different from what we’d originally imagined, but we could still demonstrate the core idea.

[Video: the phone AR demo]

[Photo: the sunlight-sensing setup]

That was probably the biggest lesson I took from this one. I’d come in wanting to apply what worked at Cal Hacks, but this project needed its own approach. Borrowing hardware didn’t work out, the glasses weren’t doing what we needed, and we had to figure out which parts of the idea we could still get in front of people.

We ended up demoing SolarScope and won Best Hardware Hack. Somehow, the project that had us moving the AR off the glasses still won a hardware prize!

My team and I were supposed to celebrate with Korean barbecue afterwards, but we never ended up going :(

Still owe ourselves that one.

items.title: Mira AI
items.note: A healthcare assistant patients can trust: it remembers each patient's context (age, state, medications) and answers safely. I led model evaluation and a three-layer prompt system with guardrails, cutting response time toward two seconds from an eleven second baseline.

items.title: JiaBot
items.note: An AI support assistant to cut pharmacy hold times. After a first version only 4% of patients tried, I led the rebuild: intent recognition instead of keywords, support cards that show each patient's refill and delivery status, and smooth handoffs to staff.

items.title: Greensort Western
items.note: London, Ontario was the largest city in Canada without a green bin, so every scrap of food waste at Western went to landfill. We launched the campus's first green bin program across residences, repurposing bins from storage, and built a sorting app (object recognition and a little gamification) into Western's student app.

items.title: Agentic Student OS
items.note: An AI operating system for students: agents that keep up with your classes, deadlines and events and take care of the busywork. A SwiftUI app on a TypeScript and Python backend.

books.name: Bookshelf: books I love
books.title: Books I love
body: These are books that I highly recommend anyone read! No spoilers so you can start fresh

items.title: Beyond the Trees
items.note:
I like two things about this book:

1. Against all odds: Without spoiling anything, I really liked Adam’s mentality and how he kept finding ways to overcome the challenges he faced.

2. The History of Canada: I love learning about history, and the book weaves a lot of First Nations history and settlers’ journeys into his own adventure, which made it even more interesting to read!

items.title: The Chip War
items.note: Highly recommend this book! It breaks down how we got to the point where compute is such a hot commodity (essentially the next oil). Even the historical parts dive into the political and economic tensions that shaped our supply chains and still influence the policies we’re dealing with today. I think its a great read to get caught up on how tech shapes geopolitics

items.title: The Call of the Wild
items.note: Read this a lot when I was younger and honestly just found the story really entertaining! I’ve always loved huskies, so the sled dogs were a big part of the appeal too. No deep explanation for this one, just a book thats nostalgic for me.

items.title: Oryx and Crake
items.note: I had to read Oryx and Crake for high school and lowkey hated it because I needed to write an essay for marks. I ended up reading a sparknotes version and pulling quotes from parts that seemed relevant for my argument.  I only gave the book a proper chance afterwards and really, really enjoyed it (goes to show I like doing things without being told to do them lol). I recently reread it, and a lot of the lessons and the metaphors reminded me of how AI is developing and how people are reacting to it.  The story moves between the past and present, slowly letting you piece together what actually happened. To think this came out in 2003, Margaret Atwood was so ahead of her time imo.

items.title: Project Hail Mary
items.note: I’m a huge space nerd, so I really enjoyed just geeking out over this story! Would definitely recommend listening to the audiobook too. The way some of the characters’ voices are brought to life makes it pretty special.

items.title: The Hunger Games
items.note: One of my favourite series! I’ve read all the books and watched all the movies so far (just waiting for Sunrise on the Reaping now). My favourite parts while reading the book was picturing the world , especially before seeing the movies, and creating my own versions of the settings in my head

items.title: The Third Door
items.note: A friend recommended The Third Door to me in first year of uni, and it was the first book that got me super into startups! It inspired me to take my first solo trip to Collision in Toronto to meet people in tech and start figuring out what my own “third door” could be. This would still be my first recommendation this to anyone interested in the startup world who’s trying to figure out the first steps to take to get involved

items.title: The Mom Test
items.note: Read this while building my startup, and a lot of the lessons were immediately applicable! It really made me think about how to ask better questions so the feedback I get is honest and useful, then figure out how to actually apply it to what I’m building. But honestly, this goes beyond startups - think just learning how to ask good questions and apply feedback is helpful for most use cases

items.title: Notion cupcake
items.note: My friend who worked at Notion asked me to bake for the team, so I made Oreo buttercream cupcakes with Notion cookies on top! Had to learn how to use a 3D printer to make a custom cookie cutter for these.

items.title: Vercel pavlova
items.note: My friend invited me to bake for Vercel! Pulled an all-nighter making these and filmed one of my first baking videos along the way. Had to figure out how to capture the process while actually getting everything baked.

items.title: Gemma cookies
items.note: Reached out to GDM (shoutout Ivan) on X, and that turned into an invite to bake cookies for the Gemma 4 launch at the top of the Transamerica Pyramid! Wanted to represent the logo of Gemma 4 so 100 cookies were frosted with the logo of Gemma

items.title: Composio Cookies
items.note: Baked Composio cookies for Composio’s booth at Hack the North! This was my first time renting out an industrial kitchen to mass produce cookies, which was a pretty cool experience. The hackers loved them, and we even had some sponsors come over to try them too!

items.title: Gemma 1B cake
items.note: The Google DeepMind team reached out to ask me to bake for Gemma’s 1 billion downloads celebration! Since it was a celebration, I decided to make a sheet cake. This took me two days and was my first time making one this large! I went with pandan because I’d recently tried kaya and pandan flavours and really wanted to incorporate them into my desserts.

items.title: Waymo cake
items.note: Got invited to bake for Sebastian Thrun, the founder of Waymo, by Adil from Silicon Mania himself (shout out to SF's first ever late night show)! Took me three days to make the entire cake, starting from the shape of the cake to the fondant itself. This was also my first time using fondant and it was a struggle to mold it into the desired shapes but ended up turning out quite nicely!
